newsitem.title: JAPAN: Scandal-hit Nomura vulnerable but still formidable.
newsitem.headline: Scandal-hit Nomura vulnerable but still formidable.

text.p: Giant Nomura Securities, hard hit by a payoff scandal that could widen further, looks more vulnerable to attack from challengers than ever before.
The brokerage will have to fight to restore credibility and woo lost clients. But experts warn against writing off Nomura as a formidable force in Japan's financial markets yet.

"Three or four years ago, the predictable response would have been that authorities won't be that hard on Nomura because who else is there," said Alicia Ogawa, financial analyst at Salomon Brothers Asia. "Now there are viable alternatives. They don't have to worry about treating Nomura with kid gloves.
"I think it would be wrong to write Nomura off, but I think it's more questionable. Japanese firms are getting used to using alternatives to the Big Four, including foreign houses."

Tokyo prosecutors last week arrested a racketeer and raided Nomura's head office one day after taking in two former Nomura executives and a third senior official suspected of violating Japan's Commercial Code and the Securities and Exchange Law with payoffs to the racketeer.
The prosecutors acted after the government's securities watchdog agency filed a criminal complaint asking that charges be considered against the executives, as well as Nomura itself.
The scandal saga -- the second to feature Nomura in just six years -- looks far from over.

Prosecutors have raided the home of ex-Nomura president Hideo Sakamaki, who resigned in March over the scandal, media said. Sakamaki has blamed the two former executives for the payments and said other executives were unaware of the deal.

Other media reports said prosecutors had searched downtown Nomura branches, apparently seeking signs of possible misdeeds linked to so-called "VIP accounts" set up for elite customers, including politicians and elite bureaucrats.

Nomura has said the estimated 8,000-9,000 "VIP accounts" were for customers regarded as needing careful treatment to avoid any illegal stock trading and were not designed to give preferential treatment to certain customers.
Some lawyers said Nomura and its former executives might decide to plead guilty, if formally charged, in an effort to put the scandal behind them as quickly as possible.

"If they plead guilty, it will take about one year to finish the court case. If not, it would take several years," said lawyer Seijiro Watanabe. "I think there is a high probability that they won't fight the case."

The brokerage also faces penalties by the Finance Ministry, expected to be stiff given Nomura's 1991 scandal record and authorities' desire to be seen cleaning up the industry ahead of its five-year "Big Bang" programme of financial deregulation.
Watanabe said the punishment would likely include suspension of part of Nomura's operations for three to six months, although its licence was not expected to be revoked.
Industry sources said some ministry officials wanted to clip Nomura's wings drastically, perhaps even to the extent of forcing it into an eventual merger with another institution.
"Nothing will really change, unless the ministry does something drastic," one source said.

Meanwhile, corporate clients and local governments are defecting, the Finance Ministry has barred the brokerage from underwriting government-backed bonds, and the Postal Life Insurance Bureau and the Postal Savings Bureau suspended business with it. Individuals are also staying away in droves.
Nomura's toughest tasks will be repairing its tattered credibility with clients and boosting battered employee morale.

"It's at a very, very critical point, but they have the potential, depending on how they spend the next year or so," said one Japanese financial specialist. "What Nomura has to do is just concentrate on getting back trust. If they can, they will obviously be number one again."
The firm employs nearly 11,000 staff in offices around the world and dominates both share and bond trading in Japan.
"The intrinsic strengths are still there," said David Threadgold, financial analyst at BZW Securities.
